scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The odzemok is a traditional solo dance for men originating in Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia.

Its name derives from the phrase 'od zeme,' translating directly to 'from the ground,' which describes the intimate relationship between the dancer's feet and the earth during the opening moments of the performance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance serves as a vibrant expression of traditional male bravado and physical agility, historically anchored in the cultural practices of Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia through both solo improvisation and structured group mock duels.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance begins with subtle foot movements close to the floor that gradually become more dramatic and fast-paced.
Dancers maintain an improvised character throughout, sometimes incorporating elements reminiscent of eastern squat dances or the Ukrainian hopak.
When performed in a large group setting, two dancers will separate from the ensemble and come together to execute a dynamic mock duel.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Composer Antonín Dvořák stands out as a notable figure who engaged with the tradition, utilizing the odzemek form to shape the first piece of his renowned Slavonic Dances Op. 72.

Regional variations span across Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia, with specific distinctions noted in prop usage: while the valaška shepherd's axe is standard in most regions, Eastern Slovak areas frequently employ a long stick instead.
The dance shares stylistic kinships and comparative elements with eastern squat dances and the Ukrainian hopak, while its musical lineage extends into 19th-century classical compositions.
